extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journalists, policymakers, and the general public tracking and identifying disinformation/news-manipulation campaigns
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and indicators used to identify, categorize, and document websites and networks that spread political disinformation (including state-linked operations, spoof sites, AI-generated content, and coordinated domain networks). Useful for investigators, reporters, and platform moderators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoofing of established outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites that impersonate or 'spoof' the names, logos, or presentation of legacy newspapers and broadcasters (e.g., 'bbc-uk.news' as a spoof of the BBC; 'bostontimes[.]org' spoofing The Boston Times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the list include many sites explicitly labeled 'Spoof of' a named outlet. Spoofing is used to lend false credibility and to mislead readers into trusting fabricated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generative AI / large language models to produce content
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites noted by researchers to have used generative AI or large language models to create articles or rewrite material from other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: franceencolere[.]fr, Verite Cachee France, and others were observed to use LLMs; Recorded Future and NewsGuard reports are cited. Indicators include unnatural phrasing, LLM prompts in content, or evidence of bulk AI-generated rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded prompts or LLM prompts visible in articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles that include prompts intended for large language models (sometimes accidentally left in titles or body text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites such as The Houston Post and others included prompts for LLMs in some of their articles—this indicates direct use of AI-generation workflows and poor editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying/reposting or aggregating content from other outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that copy, republish, or heavily repost content from other news organizations (e.g., copying from RT, ABC News, CBS News).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Albuquerque Breaking News, KBSF-San Francisco News, and Little Rock AR News. Republishing can be used to launder content and artificially amplify narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated audio/video or deepfakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing fabricated audio, video, or other manipulated media presented as real conversations or events (e.g., fabricated audio of a conversation between US officials; deepfake videos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear Story News and Miami Chronicle were accused by the U.S. federal government of publishing fabricated audio. Deepfakes are cited elsewhere (e.g., video targeting Zelensky's wife). This is a major indicator of deliberate disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or misleading site metadata / origin claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that falsely claim a long history, fake founding dates, or otherwise misrepresent their origin (e.g., claiming to exist since 1937 but registered in 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miami Chronicle falsely claimed long existence; 'About' pages with Lorem ipsum or other placeholder text are red flags for inauthentic outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of valid contact info or use of fictitious staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites that lack verifiable contact information, list fictitious journalists, or use fake author names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Miami Chronicle lacks valid contact info; Media Alternatif lists a fictitious journalist. Lack of transparent ownership and contact details suggests inauthentic operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative/mirror domains and domain rotation to evade bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation and use of alternative domains, mirrors, or rebranded domains to circumvent sanctions, bans, or takedowns (e.g., many RT alternative domains created after 2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RT alternatives (actualidad-rt[.]com, estr[.]online, swentr[.]site, etc.) illustrate how state-linked actors spin up mirror domains. Large networks of pravda-XX domains perform similar evasion and localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct links to state intelligence or state funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence or credible accusations that a site is funded, run, or materially supported by state intelligence agencies or the state (e.g., GRU, FSB), or state-linked organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: John Mark Dougan/CopyCop is described as receiving resources from the GRU; NewsFront is reported funded by the FSB; listing such links is used as a criterion for classifying sites as state-linked disinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of IDN homograph attacks to impersonate brands
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain names that use internationalized domain name (IDN) homograph tricks (replacing characters with visually similar foreign characters) to mimic established outlets (e.g., xn--theguardan-4ub[.]com).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IDN homograph attacks are explicit deception techniques; the example replaced 'i' with a Turkish 'ı' to fake 'The Guardian.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational linkage into coordinated networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that are part of named coordinated networks and campaigns (e.g., CopyCop, the Pravda network, Portal Kombat, Operation False Façade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article groups many domains under networks; network membership—shared registrants, repeated templates, common narratives—is used to identify coordinated influence operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabricated or misattributed quotes to imply intelligence involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing fabricated quotes or misattributing statements to individuals to suggest clandestine intelligence or political plots (e.g., fabricated quotes from John Scarlett implying CIA/MI6 involvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The xn--theguardan example shows fabricated quotes that serve to retroactively justify narratives about foreign interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted audience strategy and narrative tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets that are tailored to specific demographic or ideological audiences (e.g., younger and left-leaning audiences) and employ strategies to intensify political divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Now, Redfish, and Ruptly are noted to primarily target younger/left-leaning audiences and to use strategies (emotionally charged coverage, whataboutism) to worsen divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of overt propaganda strategies (e.g., whataboutism, grassroots framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics such as whataboutism, posing as grassroots or independent startups, and other overt propaganda strategies to cultivate trust and polarization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redfish presents as a 'grassroots' left-wing startup while using whataboutism and other strategies; labeling such tactics helps classify outlets as propagandistic rather than independent journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of coordination with foreign or domestic troll farms
rubrics_metrics.description: Connections to organized troll farms, node operators, or actors known for coordinated inauthentic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News of Russian troll farms and accounts (e.g., networks linked to InfoRos or Prigozhin-linked NGOs) is cited; such ties are used as evidence of coordinated disinformation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious or unverified sources and NGOs
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing NGOs or organizations that are unverified, fictitious, or known to be linked to malign actors (e.g., NGOs founded by Yevgeny Prigozhin used as sources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media Alternatif cited a Prigozhin-founded NGO for an unverified claim; using such sources is a reliability red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reused/mislabeled media assets (e.g., image filenames in another language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical artifacts in media or assets—like image filenames in Russian—suggest content origin or reuse from other-language sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Miami Chronicle had some images with filenames in Russian, which researchers flagged as evidence of content laundering or reuse across operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/monetization-driven aggregation masquerading as news
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that aggregate crime news or other sensational content primarily to monetize via social platforms, potentially mixing real and fabricated stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel3 Now was described as a commercial operation aggregating crime news to make money on social media rather than a genuine newsroom; such business motives can indicate low editorial standards and vulnerability to deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and ownership anomalies (suspicious registrars, jurisdictions, duplicate patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain registration patterns that indicate mass-registered clusters, suspicious registrars, or ownership entities with prior fraudulent behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media Alternatif's owner (Host Master, Cyprus) had a prior fraud conviction for selling confusingly similar domain names; mass registration of region-news domains (e.g., many 'news-<city>.net') is a structural indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual and region-specific cloning (mass localized sites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers of localized sites (pravda-XX, topnews.* series, news-<region>.net) created to give the appearance of local/independent outlets across languages and regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extensive lists of pravda-xx domains and topnews.* regional domains illustrate a tactic to create geographic credibility and to spread similar narratives widely across locales and languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidiary outlets and content redistribution inside state media ecosystems
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlets that are subsidiaries, shows, or mirrors of state-funded media and whose content is reposted across those ecosystems (e.g., In the Now, Redfish reposted on RT; Ruptly as an RT subsidiary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relationships show editorial control and distribution channels; labeling such ties aids in identifying state-amplified content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent researcher or government accusations / legal actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites explicitly named in government filings, U.S. Department of Justice actions, or identified by reputable research organizations as part of disinformation operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include U.S. government accusations against some sites, DOJ documents cited (doppelganger_affidavit_9.4.24.pdf), and NewsGuard/Recorded Future reports; such authoritative findings are used as classification evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deliberate misspellings or brand slighting to mimic outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain or site-name misspellings or slight alterations used to evoke a trusted brand while remaining legally distinct (e.g., 'veritecachee[.]fr' missing accents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is similar to spoofing but includes subtler misspellings and diacritic removal; it reduces detection while still invoking brand recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral pattern: rapid emergence around geopolitical events
rubrics_metrics.description: Clusters of sites or campaigns that appear or increase activity around specific geopolitical events (e.g., elections, wars) to influence public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites operations timed to the 2024 French legislative election, 2024 U.S. election cycle, and the Russo-Ukrainian War—timing and surge patterns are used as forensic indicators.
